None is a cause, and none answers a research question yet: anything causal needs designs that come after the exploration.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **eyebrow**: Stage 3 of 3 · exploratory data analysis · first pass done
- **title**: What Australia's IP data show so far, and how we know
- **lead**: This research asks how Australia's intellectual property system creates public value, and where IP Australia could add the most. Before answering, the data have been examined in three stages: every measure on its own, then every pair of measures, then the pairs that mattered with their other factors held together. These pages set out what each stage found, in plain English, and let you follow any finding back to the public data it came from.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **numbered observations, in three stages.** 231.
- **lenses (units of analysis)** 7.
- **public data sources.** 54.
- **research questions, still to answer.** 5.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text: The analysis has three stages, each looking at the same data in a new way. Stage 3's first pass is done and its two tables (early signals and data gaps) await the research owner's review. Only then, with the owner's agreement, are the five questions answered.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Each variable on its own.** Status: Complete. What each measure looks like, how complete it is, and its quirks. 128 observations (U0 to U127).
- **Pairs of variables.** Status: Complete. Which measures move together, how strongly, and for whom. 63 observations (B1 to B63).
- **Many variables together.** Status: First pass done. Whether the signals survive once other factors are held together, and what structure there is. 40 observations (M1 to M40).
- **Answering the questions.** Status: After the owner's review. The five questions, with evidence proportionate to each claim.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **id**: M1
- **intro**: Every observation can be followed from the published data to the finding, and a Stage 3 observation back to the Stage 2 signal it tests. This one shows how.
- **title**: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often, once the factors settled at filing are held
- **text**: Stage 2 found that Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 points less often (B6). Holding the route, filing year, state and co-filers together, 31.2 points of the gap remain (87.2%), in both decades. The chart sets each raw gap (grey) beside the held one (blue), with its interval. Open it to see the chain from Stage 2, the reasoning, and why this is an association and not a cause.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
What Stage 2 found

Stage 2 measured every pair of measures in each lens and kept only those that are at least small, survive the correction for the number of pairs tested, and hold in a second period or sample. Most such pairs are how the IP system works, or one broad gradient of development running through places and countries. These are the signals left once those are set aside: associations to test in Stage 3, not explanations. Stage 3 has since tested each; every one of their pages says what was left.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes.** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too. Australians' trade marks with no agent before the first renewal stay in force less often (19.1 points). The arrow may run backwards: an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: B5, B6, B10.
- **Some inventions made here are filed or held overseas.** About one patent in seven with an inventor in Australia is filed from overseas. Australian-filed patents now held only overseas are more common among the wide and the granted, though by firm the youngest filers are not clearly different. Few of the US patents citing Australian research have an Australian party, but a citation is not use, so none of this shows where value is realised. Observations: B16, B19, B26, B46.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries; the signals of value disagree.** Filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia. But they reach fewer countries and are cited less, mostly because of that reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010. Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55.
- **Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm.** Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer taken out. Areas that gained graduates or income over a decade were not seen to gain filing, so it looks like a standing difference between places. Observations: B29, B30, B58, B59.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Among firms, filing goes with company form, age and, among large employers, size and industry.** R&D spend goes with patenting only weakly, even within size bands. About half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, mostly private companies of 3 to 10 years. Counting every large employer, the largest are 24.3 points more likely than the smallest to have a filing linked, and industry sorts patenting far more than size. Observations: B22, B23, B50, B51.
- **Across countries, IP follows R&D and income.** Across OECD members, patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, and Australia filed about what its business R&D predicts in 2016 to 2020. Within a decade, changes in R&D were not seen to go with changes in patenting. Few of Australia's researchers work in business (31st of 37 members). Observations: B32, B33, B34, B61.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing.** Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. Of the changes in fees to obtain a right, only one break went the way a price would; of the changes in renewal fees, only one (trade marks, July 1993) survives every check. Observations: B37, B47, B49.
- **Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer.** From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals'. Observations: B17, B18.
- **Across industries, the patents allocated by technology follow R&D once services are counted.** Industry counts are applications allocated by what they protect, not what each industry's businesses file. Through the crosswalk with services, patents allocated per business follow business R&D per business. A division's share of innovating businesses showed no clear pattern with patenting in three surveys. Observations: B53, B54, B42, B60.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text: - **Institutions whose research US patents cite more also patent more.** Larger, more cited universities file more patents per work. Across institutions, disclosures seemed to go with patents and patents with licence income, but that came from dividing every measure by the same research spend: at the same spend, Stage 3 finds patents do not go with licence income (M24). No association was detected between industry-partnered grants and joint filing, though a moderate one is not ruled out. Observations: B44, B45, B62, M24.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
Read together, Stage 1's observations point to a handful of patterns. Each is descriptive: a shape in the data worth testing, not an explanation. The numbers link to the observations behind them.

- **Patents are mostly filed from overseas; trade marks mostly from home.** About nine in ten standard patents filed in Australia come from overseas (the United States alone 43.6%), while Australians file 59.19% of trade marks. China now files as many patent applications here as Australians do, and three-quarters of Australians' own applications are made abroad. Observations: U13, U70, U93.
- **Almost everything is concentrated.** The top 1% of filing firms filed 55.3% of firms' standard patents; the tenth of postal areas with the most patents filed 72.5% of them with 29.2% of the people; five attorney firms handle 63.96% of standard patents; the Group of Eight hold two-thirds of ARC and NHMRC funding. Observations: U44, U52, U21, U83.
- **Places differ far more than chance would make them.** 68.2% to 72.5% of areas file below what chance allows around the national rate, and 6.7% to 15.5% above it, in small areas and pooled ones alike. Later stages must model this spread rather than assume it away. Observations: U53.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney.** Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone. Observations: U20, U48.
- **Provisional applications doubled in FY2026.** 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia. Observations: U8.
- **Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses.** Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need. Observations: U28, U3.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Later standard patents more often stay in force; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years.** Standard patents' median time in force rose from 10.6 years (granted in the 1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). These are shares still on the register, not value; the research owner adopted years in force as a working measure for Stage 2, alongside other signals. Observations: U36.
- **US patents often cite Australian research, and R&D spending has fallen.** US patents often cite Australian research institutions' work; 93.6% of those citations come from patents with no Australian applicant or inventor, as most US patents have none. A citation is not use. Australia's R&D spending rose to 2008 as a share of GDP and has fallen since, below the OECD median. Observations: U85, U65, U66.
- **The register's history shapes what it can say.** Early years hold only the rights that survived until records were computerised; some events were dated in batches; patent ownership history starts in FY2003. Each is handled, but each limits comparisons over time. Observations: U23, U17, U34.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text: - **Links between datasets are the weakest point.** Firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID links fewer recent filers to a business number (IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs); only large employers have an industry; half the universities' patents carry a postcode that is not a place where people live. Observations: U41, U45, U75, U87.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text: Every observation page has the same parts, and each part looks different, so that a finding is never confused with the reasoning, assumptions or limits around it.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **The observation.** The finding itself, in a green box with its number (U0 to U127 in Stage 1, B1 to B63 in Stage 2, M1 to M40 in Stage 3). Only this is a finding.
- **Reasoning steps.** How the data lead to the finding, one step at a time, in dashed grey. Steps are not findings.
- **Assumptions.** Where the analysis takes something as given. Marked in amber, so you can judge them.
- **Limits.** What the observation cannot tell you, in rose.
- **Explainers.** Statistical or technical terms, explained in blue beside the text, and on any dotted word.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text: The research goal asks every claim to say how strong its evidence is. There are four levels. Everything in Stage 1 is the first; most of Stages 2 and 3 is the second.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
- **Descriptive.** Stages: 1; 2; 3. What the data show. How much, how often, for whom. No claim about why.
- **Observational.** Stages: 2; 3. Things go together, even with other factors held. There may be other explanations. Stages 2 and 3 produce these.
- **Causal.** One thing causes another. Needs a design, such as a natural experiment, that this exploration does not have.
- **Projected.** An estimate of the future, with its assumptions stated. Belongs to Question 5.
title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far

text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.
title: What Stage 3 found

text:
- **Filing without an attorney still goes with far fewer grants.** With the route, year, state and co-filers held together, Australian individuals' patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often (35.8 raw), in both decades; trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it. Not a cause: an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: M1, M2.
- **Australian organisations' patents: three readings that still disagree.** At the same reach they are less likely to end (hazard ratios 0.648 to 0.811), yet they reach fewer offices and are cited about 27% to 30% less at the same reach, field, route and year. None of the three is value; they must be read together. Observations: M3, M4.
title: What Stage 3 found

text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.
title: What Stage 3 found

text:
- **Fees look a weak lever.** Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would. Observations: M28, M34.
- **Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly.** Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points. Observations: M8, M9, M11, M29.
- **Places: one advantage gradient, and what lies beyond it.** Advantage, income and education are mostly one measure. Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays. Observations: M13, M14, M31, M32.
title: What Stage 3 found

text:
- **Across countries and industries, patents follow business R&D.** Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; across industries, patents allocated per business follow business R&D at the same value added. Australia is nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on non-IP indicators. Observations: M17, M18, M22.
- **Institutions: research that patents cite goes with their own patenting; licence income does not follow patents.** Across every kind of institution, with kind and size held, research that patents cite goes with more patents per work. At the same research spend, more patents are not seen to go with more licence income. Observations: M38, M24.
- **Raising the Bar's rush holds; the business cycle barely shows.** With trend and season held, Raising the Bar's rush and Australians' lower level of patents after it hold, while the Designs Act's step does not stand apart from a control. With block resampling, the cycle shows only in overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008. Trade marks share a long-run path with real GDP and run a quarter ahead of it, as IP Australia's note finds, but the lead is small once GDP's own growth is held and is not detected since 2008. Observations: M25, M36, M19, M39.
title: What Stage 3 found

text:
Every Stage 3 page follows the same five steps, and shows the first three at its top as a chain: what Stage 2 found, what was held together, and what is left.

- **Start from a Stage 2 signal.** Signal. Sub-questions: A pair that held in two samples. A pair of measures that went together in Stage 2, in a first sample and again in a second: for example, filing without an attorney and fewer grants (B6).
- **Name its third factors.** Third factors. Sub-questions: What else could explain it. Stage 2 named, for each signal, the other factors that could make the two measures go together: the route of filing, the year, the field, the filer's type, a place's advantage.
- **Hold them together.** Held. Sub-questions: One model, every factor at once. One model holds every named factor fixed at once, so the signal is read among rights, firms or places alike in all of them. Intervals allow a filer's many rights to be alike, or resample neighbouring quarters in blocks.
- **Compare raw and held.** Compare. Sub-questions: How much of the signal is left. The raw figure (Stage 2's comparison, with nothing held) is set beside the held one. The charts show both: grey for raw, blue for held, each with its 95% interval.
title: What Stage 3 found

text: - **Give the outcome, and check it again.** Outcome. Sub-questions: Holds, weakened, not detected…. title: What Stage 3 found

text:
Besides testing signals, Stage 3 asked which measures repeat each other and whether there are distinct kinds of place or country. These are descriptive.

- **Places' characteristics are mostly one advantage gradient.** Across 2,525 postal areas the first component, advantage, carries 49.5% of the variation, and IRSAD can be predicted almost entirely from the other measures. No single measure (income, education) should be read as the one that matters. Observations: M13.
- **Places form a continuum, not kinds.** The best grouping of areas has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments; one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas holds 56% of the placed standard patents. Observations: M16.
- **Countries differ along several dimensions.** Across 35 OECD members the first component carries 24.7% of the variation. Australia is low on manufacturing and exports, high on education and new businesses, and nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden. Observations: M17.
- **Trends dominate the monthly series.** Trade marks' and overseas applicants' series are almost all trend; seasons are strong for provisionals and Australians' trade marks; what is left of different series moves together only moderately, perhaps the calendar. Observations: M20.

Applied, it closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to an ABN and changes no firm finding. Adopting it is the owner's decision (OQ26). Observations: M12, U126.

title: What Stage 3 found

text:
- **holds**: The same direction as the raw figure, its 95% interval clear of no difference, and at least half of the raw size left once the third factors are held together.
- **weakened**: The same direction and clear of no difference, but less than half of the raw size left, so much of the signal was its third factors.
- **not detected once held**: The interval with the factors held includes no difference. Not the same as no association; a moderate one may be missed.
- **reversed**: Clear of no difference, but the other way round from the raw figure.
- **appears once held**: The raw figure was not detected, but with the factors held an association is clear.
- **not detected either way**: Neither the raw nor the held figure is clear of no difference.
- **does not replicate**: Clear in one sample or period but not in the second, so not carried as a signal.
- **mixed**: The page's parts differ (one group or period holds, another does not); its text says which is which.
- **refined**: A description that sharpens or corrects an earlier one, rather than a test of a held signal.
title: What Stage 3 found

text: The three stages are groundwork. They are honest about what they are: a careful description of each measure on its own, then of which measures go together, then of how much of each link is left once its other factors are held. This page gathers what they cannot do, the assumptions they make, where the data are weakest, and the mistakes found and corrected on the way.
title: Limits and assumptions

section: What the three stages cannot tell you
text:
- **Why.** Stage 1's observations are descriptive and Stage 2's are associations. Stage 3 holds the measured third factors together, which is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain a link, and some links may run backwards (an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney, B6, M1). Causal claims need designs, such as natural experiments, that come after the exploration.
- **What "not detected" means.** When Stage 3 says a link is not detected once held, its interval includes no difference. That is not evidence of no link: with 19 industries, about 40 universities or 36 countries, a moderate link can go undetected. Only for patents' renewal at each anniversary is the null precise (within about 1.4 points, M28).
- **Value.** Counts of rights, lifetimes, reach and citations are measures of activity and private value, not of public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.
- **People from places.** Stage 2's pairs across postal areas and countries describe the areas and countries, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more; that does not show the graduates are the filers.
title: Limits and assumptions

section: What the three stages cannot tell you
text:
- **Small units.** Industries (19 divisions), OECD members (36 to 38) and research institutions (about 40 universities, 60 to 84 institutions) are few, so their intervals are wide and their results are leads at most; a second period of the same units is a stability check, not a replication.
- **Everyone.** The firms lens holds businesses found in an IP, R&D, procurement or tax source, not all businesses, so shares of large employers that file are taken over every employer (B50). Individuals in IP RAPID are pseudonymised, so their gender cannot be estimated; only inventors' can, from names, and reliably only for inventors in Australia.
- **Small firms.** Size and industry are known only for employers of 100 or more (WGEA). Without the ABS's BLADE (linked business data, ruled out for now), small firms' size, industry, growth and survival are out of reach (OQ20). This limits how far Questions 3 and 5 can be answered.
- **The present.** The latest months of some records are incomplete because the register records them late (trade mark and design cessations, recent ABN links, perhaps priority claims, B38). Each observation says which years are safe to compare.
title: Limits and assumptions

text:
- Public data are taken to be what their publishers say they are. Where checks found otherwise (placeholder dates, mislabelled countries, numbers counted twice), the data were repaired and the repair recorded; elsewhere, the publisher's values stand.
- A business is identified by its ABN. Related companies in a group have different ABNs and are counted apart.
- A place is a postal area, reached through the postcode recorded on an application or in the business register. A registered address may be a head office or an adviser's, not where the work is done.
- An industry is reached through what a right protects (its technology or goods classes), by published probabilities, because few firms in the corpus have an industry.
- Gender is estimated from first names and countries, as a probability summed over many people; it says nothing about any one person, and is read only for inventors in Australia.
- Money is shown as recorded (nominal) unless a page says otherwise; fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the quarterly Consumer Price Index.
- Where a series begins with only the survivors of an earlier system, or with partial records, those years are left out rather than estimated.
title: Limits and assumptions

text:
- Stage 2 measures every pair on one scale from 0 to 1 and calls a pair a lead only if it reaches 0.1, survives the correction for the number of pairs, holds in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure (ADR 0030).
- Stage 3 calls a signal held if, with its third factors held together, it keeps its direction, its 95% interval is clear of no difference and at least half of its raw size is left (ADR 0046). A filer's rights are one source of evidence (clustered by the filer's party), and quarterly changes are resampled in blocks.
title: Limits and assumptions

text:
The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

- **Firms.** Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID's recent filings carry fewer, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs (U41, U45, U100). A name match recovers most of the rest and changes no firm finding, but is kept apart from the counts (M12). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more (U112), the main third factor every firm signal lacks.
- **Industries.** Industries reach patents only through a crosswalk; the recommended one leaves out services, so a second one with services sits beside it (U75, U114).
- **Places.** Places reach IP only through postcodes, and half the universities' patents carry a postcode where no one lives (U49, U87).
- **Institutions.** Research institutions reach their IP through a reviewed list of names and business numbers that someone in the sector has yet to check (U81, OQ11).
title: Limits and assumptions

text: - **Inventors and families.** Inventors' countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad, gender only as an estimate that holds for Australia (U95, U97), and older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete before FY2010 (B55, OQ21).

title: What comes next

text: - **Stage 2, pairs of variables.** When: Complete (28 October 2026; reviewed 2 November) Asks: Which pairs of measures move together, in what shape, how strongly, and for whom? How: Within each lens, every pair of variables was screened on one scale. A pair counted as a lead only if it was at least small, survived the correction for the number of pairs tested, and held in a second period or sample; the planned pairs were then measured in plain units, with intervals. Example: Postal areas with more advantaged residents file 1.7 to 1.9 times as many standard patents per person for each step of advantage, and the gradient is not one firm's (B29, B30). Adds: The first **observational** evidence: associations that bear on who benefits (Q2) and on the conditions for value (Q3), each with its candidate third factors. Done when: Every pair within each lens screened; each lead with its size and interval, past the correction and held in a second sample.
title: What comes next

text: - **Stage 3, many variables together.** When: First pass done (3 November 2026); tables await the owner's review. Asks: Do the signals survive once other factors are held together? What structure and groups exist? How: Each signal Stage 2 carried was modelled with its named third factors held together, and its raw and held figures compared (holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed). The methods the final review asked for were used throughout: intervals that allow a filer's rights to be alike, block resampling of quarterly changes, citations counted at a fixed age, industry comparisons through the crosswalk with services, and research spend as a base. Places' and countries' characteristics were reduced to a few components, and places grouped to see whether they form kinds. Example: Is an area's patent rate still linked to advantage once its business mix and education are allowed for? Yes, but weaker: 35% to 39% of the ratio is left, and business density and degrees beyond resources matter too (M14). Adds: Separates signals that hold from ones explained by something else, and produces two tables: fifteen early signals, with their evidence and strength, and thirteen data gaps, with possible sources and costs. Done when: When the owner has reviewed the two tables and decided on the name match (OQ26).

text: - **Answering the questions.** When: After the owner's review, with the owner's agreement. Asks: The five research questions. How: Analyses designed for each question: descriptive where that suffices, and natural experiments or other designs wherever an additional benefit is claimed. Example: Using Raising the Bar as a natural experiment, following who rushed and what their rushed applications became, to estimate what a policy actually changed (M25). Adds: Answers with evidence proportionate to each claim, as the research goal requires. Done when: When the owner adopts the findings.

Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed or narrowed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 (U67), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 (U34), by IP Australia's own register (U103); most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (B11), by a gap in older records (B55); and about half of the recent fall in first patent filers, by the name match (M12).

- Firms with a first observed patent fell from 1,167 (FY2021) to 810 (FY2024); innovation patents closed in August 2021 (U45). About half of the later fall is linking (M12).

text: Every observation on the atlas should be the best current reading of the data. Whenever an observation is added or changed, or the data and outputs beneath it change, it is compared straight away with the observations nearest to it, and each pair is judged: one supports, refines, contests, outmodes or disproves the other, or they do not bear on each other. This page shows what those checks have found. An observation that a later one outmodes or disproves is marked at once and proposed for retirement; it leaves the atlas only when the research owner approves, and the ledger below keeps it, with what replaced it.
title: Keeping the atlas current

text:
- **Find the nearest observations.** A search reads the new or changed observation three ways: its words (a keyword match), its meaning (a small language model run locally, free), and its structure (the columns, sources and terms it uses). The closest ones, and any it names or that name it, are its candidates.
- **Judge each pair.** Claude reads the two observations together and records one of six judgements, with a reason: none, supports, refines, contests (with what would settle it), outmodes or disproves.
- **Keep it on record.** Each observation's check is stored with a fingerprint of what it rests on: its own words, the outputs above it, its data files, and the observations it names. If any of these change, the check is out of date and the atlas will not build until it is redone. When the data beneath an observation change, its analysis is run again, or the reason it cannot be affected is written down.
- **Correct what is partly out of date.** When a later observation overturns one claim in an observation that otherwise stands, the wording is corrected in place with a dated note that quotes what it said, and the later result is shown in a box under it.
title: Keeping the atlas current

text: - **Ask before removing anything.** Outmoded and disproven observations are marked at once and listed above. Only the research owner's recorded approval retires one; until then it stays, marked as superseded.
title: Keeping the atlas current

text: - B62 outmoded by M24: B62 reads its links between disclosures, patents and licence income as holding in both periods, but they were correlations of measures all divided by the same research budget. M24 compares institutions at the same research spend and finds disclosures go with patents, and patents with start-ups, in 2010 to 2015 only, and patents with licences and licence income in neither period. M24 says everything B62 says that still stands.
title: Keeping the atlas current

text:
- M22 and B40: B40 finds industries with more business R&D per business receive more trade marks per business. M22 finds that link shrinks once value added per business is allowed for (0.423 and 0.392 against 0.609 and 0.582), with likely ranges that just include zero, so it may be output rather than R&D. What would settle it: Business R&D for more years than 2023–24, or a finer industry level than the 19 divisions, to narrow the likely range; or the same test on another year's value added.
- M36 and B56: B56 finds economic growth goes with overseas applicants' patents, more strongly from 2008. M36 allows for neighbouring quarters behaving alike and finds neither period's link clear (0.158 and 0.380), which points against B56 without ruling the link out. What would settle it: A test of whether growth leads overseas patent filing, with lags, over the longest series (as M39 does for trade marks).

text: - M38 and M23: M38 finds, across every kind of institution, that research patents cite goes with more patents per work in both periods with kind, size, citations and grants held. M38 notes the difference; neither settles whether the link holds within universities in 2017 to 2023. What would settle it: M38's model fitted to the 40 universities alone for 2017 to 2023, or with the kind of institution allowed to change the patent-cited link; the institutions link itself awaits review (OQ11).

Checked against IP Australia

IP Australia publishes its own figures on the IP system every year, in its Australian IP Reports, and its own research. This review checks the observations against them: where IP Australia has published the same thing, do the two agree? Where it has drawn a conclusion, what does the evidence here add?

**Two passes, one record.** The review of 27 October 2026 checked Stage 1's observations U0 to U98; on 4 November 2026 the same check was made of the observations since (U99 to U127, and Stages 2 and 3), and of the two tests it led to (M39, M40), so all 231 now have a verdict. Neither pass changed an observation. Since then, IP Australia's own register has settled one of its four disagreements and narrowed another, and the observations it bore on were restated in the notebook beside their first wording, at the research owner's decision. Each verdict below is as the review gave it; "Since the review" and the notes on each disagreement say where things now stand.

text:
- **Find what IP Australia has published.** Its twelve Australian IP Reports (2015 to 2026), its research papers and its analytic notes, as the project's companion repository holds them, page by page. text: - **Keep it checkable.** The 195 figures, each with its report and page, and the code that recounts them, are kept in the repository. A test fails if they fall out of step with the data.

text:
- **corroborated**: IP Australia publishes the same figure, and Stage 1's data reproduce it once both count it the same way.
- **consistent**: IP Australia publishes a related figure or finding that points the same way, but not the same figure.
- **qualified**: IP Australia's figures agree, but show a caveat the observation does not state.
- **disputed**: IP Australia gives a figure for what reads as the same thing, and Stage 1's data cannot reproduce it.
- **contradicted**: IP Australia's figure disagrees, and no difference in how it was counted explains it.
- **not testable**: IP Australia has published nothing that can be compared.

section: IP Australia's conclusions and what the evidence adds
text:
What IP Australia concludes, how strongly it says it, and what the evidence here adds (C1 to C12 from the first review; C13 to C16 from the second). None of IP Australia's conclusions is adopted here: that is the research owner's decision.

- **C1: The rise in provisional applications reflects digital tools, including AI, lowering the cost of a first filing.** Strength: "Consistent with"; "an important focus for ongoing analysis". Adds: U8: the rise is broad (single-filing individuals 1,538 to 2,507) and concentrated (54 individuals filed 1,528). Both fit; neither proves it. Since then, FY2025's fall in provisionals followed up within 12 months (6.66%, against 12.24% to 14.15% in FY2022 to FY2024) shows at every filing volume, steepest among heavy individual filers (B38, M35).
- **C2: A firm's first patent or trade mark coincides with lasting gains in income and productivity.** Strength: "Dynamic associations, not definitive causal effects." Adds: Nothing to test. Stage 1 has no data on firms' performance.
title: Checked against IP Australia

section: IP Australia's conclusions and what the evidence adds
text: - **C3: Patents whose examination is sped up are renewed, used in products and built on more.** Strength: Research commissioned by IP Australia; an association. Adds: U34 (expedited requests, 1.87% to 10.31%) and U36 (years in force) are the same two measures: a pair for Stage 2 that would repeat the finding with open data. Stage 2 found expedited patents slightly more often in force after 10 years, pooled, in both periods; the link differs by filer and is not explained by who asks, and "expedited" mixes urgent requests with work-sharing (B13). Stage 3 held the filer, field, route, cohort, co-filers and classes together: the link is not detected in FY2010 to FY2016 (a hazard ratio of 1.021) and reverses in FY2003 to FY2009 (1.124), and Australian individuals' expedited patents are more likely to end in both periods (M5). The open data do not repeat the study's finding. On the study's own wider measure, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents against its 41.9%), patents are more likely to end too, held together (1.276 and 1.383; M40).
title: Checked against IP Australia

section: IP Australia's conclusions and what the evidence adds
text:
- **C4: The innovation patent did not meet its goal of serving small businesses.** Strength: IP Australia's and the Productivity Commission's research. Adds: U7: Australians' share of second-tier patents fell from 79.2% to 87.4% (FY1990 to FY2010) to about one in six in FY2021, when overseas applicants filed before the closure.
- **C5: Raising the Bar increased competition and follow-on invention, unevenly across fields.** Strength: Research commissioned by IP Australia. Adds: U28 and U33 show the rush and the early examination requests that any evaluation must allow for. With trend and season held, the rush (0.605 in logs) and a lower level after it (-0.334) hold (M25).
- **C6: Clutter on the trade mark register is not an immediate concern, though falling renewals are a possible source.** Strength: IP Australia's own measures. Adds: U36 shows the fall in the share of trade marks still in force after ten years; Stage 1 cannot measure whether marks are used.

Overseas applicants' trade marks move against unemployment (-0.561, then -0.224), as the note would expect; Australians' trade marks move against employment.
